item.title: A new website
item.description:
The website got a makeover: faster, phone-friendly, and now with a dark mode for late-night reading of papers.

There is also a spin on the home page that will happily precess for you. Unlike the ones in the lab, it never decoheres.

item.title: Public talk: when spins learn to compute
item.description:
I gave a public talk in the series Faszination Mathematik und Physik of the University of Augsburg, in the Zeughaus Augsburg: Wenn Spins rechnen lernen – Auf dem Weg zu skalierbaren Quantencomputern (when spins learn to compute: on the way to scalable quantum computers).

Quantum computers promise computing power beyond today’s computers, but for that single qubits have to get better and millions of them have to work together. Since all classical computers are built on semiconductor chips, it makes sense to build quantum computers from semiconductors too, with qubits made from the spin of single electrons. The talk followed these spins as they learn to compute, one trick at a time.

item.title: Humboldt Research Fellowship for Beatriz Pérez González
item.description:
Congratulations to Beatriz Pérez González, who has won a Humboldt Research Fellowship from the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation! Beatriz joined our group in 2024, and since March 2026 she continues her research here as a Humboldt fellow.

She studies what happens when light and matter interact strongly in semiconductor spin qubits, and how microwave photons could link qubits that sit far apart on a chip. Her theoretical models look for realistic devices in which this regime can be reached and put to use.

item.title: Professor at the University of Augsburg
item.description:
Since April 2023 I am professor for Quantum Information and Quantum Computing at the University of Augsburg, where I had already been an interim professor in 2021. With the Emmy Noether programme of the German Research Foundation (DFG) I am building up a junior research group here.

The university introduced its newly appointed professors, me among them: Neu nach Augsburg berufen (in German).

item.title: Open positions
item.description:
From April 2023 I will be a professor at the University of Augsburg and I am inviting motivated scientists to join our group to work on Quantum information theory based on solid state spin qubits. We have two PhD positions and two postdoc positions.

PhD positions: Theoretical modeling and simulation of spin qubits in quantum dots. Send your CV, letter of motivation, and the name and contact data from a possible reference by email. Feel free to contact me for further information!

item.title: An electron bus for nuclear spin entanglement
item.description:
Our article has been published in Physical Review Applied and highlighted as Editors’ Suggestion.

Entangled states of matter are a crucial resource for many quantum tasks, but producing such states deterministically between noninteracting parties is quite challenging, especially in solid-state systems. Here researchers offer a protocol to entangle two ensembles of nuclear spins that surround two quantum dots connected by an electron waveguide, employing sequential interaction of the nuclei with spin-polarized electrons. The authors numerically demonstrate the efficacy of the protocol, even in disordered and noisy setups, which suggests its feasibility with state-of-the-art techniques in quantum information processing.

item.title: Emmy Noether group: a spin-based Floquet quantum processor
item.description:
The German Research Foundation (DFG) will fund my Emmy Noether junior research group Spin-based Floquet quantum information processor.

Spin qubits in semiconductor quantum dots are a promising route to large quantum computers, but they still suffer from charge noise and only interact with their nearest neighbours. The idea of the project is to put time to work: qubits driven periodically in time (Floquet engineering) can be placed where noise hardly reaches them, switched on and off for long-distance couplings, used to probe the noise itself, and even organised into time crystals that keep their order while computing.
